lessons.title: Represent Polygons on the Coordinate Plane
lessons.objective: I can draw polygons from their vertex coordinates on the coordinate plane, and use coordinates to find side lengths and solve perimeter and area problems.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain how I found a distance using the words vertices, coordinates, and absolute value.

concept.heading: The coordinates already know the side lengths
concept.intro: Graph the points, connect them in order, and the polygon appears. Then the same coordinates that placed the corners tell you exactly how long each side is.
concept.keyIdea: Polygons on the Coordinate Plane. 1. Plot all given vertices and connect them in order to form the polygon. 2. Find side lengths by counting grid units or using coordinate distance formulas. 3. Perimeter = Sum of all side lengths; Area = Use standard polygon formulas

worked.title: Watch me find one side
lines: (-4.5, 3) and (5, 3) share y = 3, so the side between them is horizontal.
Its length is the distance between the x-coordinates: |5 − (−4.5)| = 9.5 units.
(5, 3) and (5, -3.75) share x = 5, so that side is vertical: |3 − (−3.75)| = 6.75 units.
linesEs: (-4.5, 3) y (5, 3) comparten y = 3, así que el lado entre ellos es horizontal.
Su longitud es la distancia entre las coordenadas x: |5 − (−4.5)| = 9.5 unidades.
(5, 3) y (5, -3.75) comparten x = 5, así que ese lado es vertical: |3 − (−3.75)| = 6.75 unidades.

together.title: Let's finish the perimeter together
lines: The shape is a rectangle, so the opposite sides match: two sides of 9.5 and two of 6.75.
That is why two of the terms are multiplied by 2 — each length appears on two sides.
linesEs: La figura es un rectángulo, así que los lados opuestos coinciden: dos lados de 9.5 y dos de 6.75.
Por eso dos de los términos se multiplican por 2 — cada longitud aparece en dos lados.

vocabulary.definition: A corner point of a polygon, named by an ordered pair on the coordinate plane.
vocabulary.example: The park's corner at (2, 4) — one corner, named by an ordered pair.

vocabulary.definition: A closed figure made of line segments; on the plane you draw it by plotting the vertices and connecting them in order.
vocabulary.example: Plot (2, 4), (5, 4), (5, −4), (2, −4) and join them — a rectangle appears.

vocabulary.definition: The total distance around a polygon — the sum of all its side lengths.
vocabulary.example: 2(9.5) + 2(6.75) = 32.5 units around the deck.

vocabulary.definition: When two vertices share an x- or y-coordinate, the distance between them is the absolute difference of the other coordinates.
vocabulary.example: (2, 4) and (5, 4) share y, so the side is |5 − 2| = 3 units.

vocabulary.definition: What one grid unit stands for in the real situation.
vocabulary.example: Each grid unit = 100 feet, so 8 units of map is 800 real feet.

vocabulary.definition: The distance between two vertices that are joined by a side.
vocabulary.example: Found with absolute value when the points share a coordinate.

lessons.title: Ordered Pairs in All Four Quadrants
lessons.objective: I can plot ordered pairs in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words quadrant, negative coordinate, reflection, and axis.

concept.heading: How do you plot points in all four quadrants?
concept.intro: The coordinate plane has four parts called quadrants. A negative coordinate means you move left (for x) or down (for y) from the origin instead of right or up.
concept.keyIdea: The Four Quadrants. Formula: Quadrant I: (+, +) | Quadrant II: (−, +) | Quadrant III: (−, −) | Quadrant IV: (+, −). 1. Quadrant I: Upper-right (+, +). 2. Quadrant II: Upper-left (−, +). 3. Quadrant III: Lower-left (−, −); Quadrant IV: Lower-right (+, −)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I will plot (-3, -4). I start at the origin (0, 0).
The x is -3, which is negative, so I move 3 units to the LEFT.
The y is -4, which is negative, so I move 4 units DOWN. I place my dot.
Both coordinates are negative, so the point is in Quadrant III.
linesEs: Voy a marcar (-3, -4). Empiezo en el origen (0, 0).
La x es -3, que es negativa, así que me muevo 3 unidades a la izquierda.
La y es -4, que es negativa, así que me muevo 4 unidades hacia abajo. Coloco mi punto.
Las dos coordenadas son negativas, así que el punto está en el cuadrante III.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Now let's plot (-5, 2). The x is -5, so which way do we move? Left 5 units.
The y is 2, which is positive, so which way? Up 2 units.
Left and up lands us in which quadrant? Quadrant II.
linesEs: Ahora marquemos (-5, 2). La x es -5, entonces ¿hacia dónde nos movemos? 5 unidades a la izquierda.
La y es 2, que es positiva, entonces ¿hacia dónde? 2 unidades hacia arriba.
A la izquierda y hacia arriba nos deja en ¿qué cuadrante? El cuadrante II.

vocabulary.term: Ordered Pairs in All Four Quadrants
vocabulary.definition: Points written as (x, y) whose positive or negative coordinates place them in one of four quadrants.
vocabulary.example: (−3, 4) is in Quadrant II.

vocabulary.definition: One of the four parts of a coordinate grid, numbered I to IV.
vocabulary.example: I (+, +) top-right, II (-, +) top-left, III (-, -) bottom-left, IV (+, -) bottom-right

vocabulary.definition: A coordinate less than zero. It means left or below the center point.
vocabulary.example: (-3, 2) means 3 left and 2 up from the origin

vocabulary.definition: A flipped, mirror image across a line.
vocabulary.example: (3, 2) reflected over the y-axis is (-3, 2) — same distance, opposite side

vocabulary.definition: One of the two number lines that frame a graph: the x-axis runs across, the y-axis runs up and down.
vocabulary.example: The x-axis goes left-right; the y-axis goes up-down; they cross at (0, 0)

vocabulary.definition: Whole numbers and their opposites, like -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.

title: Grid Architects

investigate: Use the two control points as opposite corners. Name the other corners.
Find width and height from coordinate differences.
Move the whole rectangle across an axis without changing its dimensions. What stays fixed?
create: Design a rectangular park crossing both axes. List the four ordered pairs and prove its perimeter and area using coordinate distances.

support.prompt: Vertices (-4.5, 3) and (5, 3) share y = 3. What is the distance between them?
support.explanation: They differ only in x: |5 − (−4.5)| = 5 + 4.5 = 9.5 units.
feedback: That subtracts 4.5 − 4 or similar — remember the point is at NEGATIVE 4.5, so the distance crosses zero.
That subtracts 5 − 3.5 or mixes an x with a y — use the two x-coordinates only.
That ignores the .5 on −4.5.
hints: Which coordinate is the same? Which differs?
The x-values are −4.5 and 5.
Distance crosses zero: 4.5 to reach 0, then 5 more.

support.prompt: Vertices (5, 3) and (5, -3.75) share x = 5. What is the distance between them?
support.explanation: They differ only in y: |3 − (−3.75)| = 3 + 3.75 = 6.75 units.
feedback: That subtracts 3.75 − 3 as if both were on the same side of zero.
5 is the shared x-coordinate, not a distance.
That adds 5 + 3.75, mixing the shared x into the answer.
hints: Which coordinate differs?
The y-values are 3 and −3.75.
3 above zero plus 3.75 below zero.

support.prompt: What is the perimeter of the rectangle with side lengths 9.5 and 6.75 units?
feedback: 16.25 is 9.5 + 6.75 — that walks only two of the four sides.
26 misses the decimal halves; recompute 19 + 13.5.
64.125 is 9.5 × 6.75 — that is the area, not the perimeter.
hints: A rectangle has four sides.
Each length appears twice.

support.prompt: Why are two of the terms multiplied by 2 in the perimeter calculation?
choices: Because perimeter always doubles the area
Because there are two coordinates in each ordered pair
A rectangle's opposite sides are equal, so each length appears on two sides
support.explanation: The two 9.5 sides and the two 6.75 sides each come in pairs — that is what the 2 counts.
feedback: Perimeter and area are different measurements; neither doubles the other.
The 2 counts sides, not coordinates.
No rounding is happening — 32.5 is exact.
hints: Walk the rectangle: how many 9.5 sides?
Two of each length.
The 2 counts the matching sides.

support.prompt: A square has vertices (1, 2), (6, 2), (6, -3), (1, -3). Find one side length and the perimeter.
support.explanation: From (1, 2) to (6, 2): |6 − 1| = 5 units. A square has four equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 × 5 = 20 units.

support.prompt: In which quadrant is the point (-4, 5)?
support.explanation: The x-coordinate is negative (left) and the y-coordinate is positive (up). Left and up is Quadrant II.
feedback: Quadrant I is where x is positive and y is positive. Check the sign of each coordinate in the point and match both.
Quadrant III holds points where both coordinates are negative. Here the y-coordinate is 5, which is positive.
Quadrant IV pairs a positive x with a negative y. Look again at the sign of the x-coordinate in (-4, 5).
hints: Look at the signs: x = -4 is negative and y = 5 is positive.
Negative x means move LEFT; positive y means move UP. Ask which corner of the plane is left-and-up.
From the origin, slide left 4 and climb up 5. Quadrants count I, II, III, IV counterclockwise from top-right.

support.prompt: A point has a positive x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate. Which quadrant is it in?
support.explanation: Positive x (right) and negative y (down) = Quadrant IV (bottom-right).
feedback: Quadrant I is where x is positive and y is positive. Check the sign of each coordinate in the point and match both.
Quadrant II needs a negative x-coordinate. This point's x is positive, so it sits on the right side of the plane.
In Quadrant III both coordinates are negative, but only the y-coordinate is negative here.
hints: Positive x pushes you RIGHT; negative y drops you DOWN.
Find the corner that is right of the y-axis and below the x-axis. Quadrants I–IV go counterclockwise from top-right.
Try a sample point like (3, -2): go right 3, then down 2. See which corner of the grid that lands in.

support.prompt: Which point is located on the x-axis?
support.explanation: A point is on the x-axis when its y-coordinate is 0. (4, 0) is on the x-axis.
feedback: Not quite. A point is on the x-axis when its y-coordinate is ___.
You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Neither coordinate is 0, so this point sits inside a quadrant rather than on an axis. A point on an axis has a coordinate of 0.
hints: A point ON the x-axis never moves up or down — its height is zero.
Check each pair's y-coordinate (the second number). On the x-axis, the y must be 0.
Read the second number in each pair. A point sits on the x-axis only when that number is 0.

steps: Problem: Name the quadrant for the point (-2, 5).
Student thinking: The x is -2, so I move 2 units DOWN. The y is 5, so I move 5 units to the RIGHT.
Student answer: (-2, 5) is in Quadrant IV.
support.explanation: The signs were matched to the wrong axis. A negative x moves LEFT (not down), and a positive y moves UP (not right). So move 2 units LEFT and 5 units UP. Left and up is Quadrant II, not Quadrant IV.
hints: Which coordinate controls left/right, and which controls up/down? The x is always the left/right move.
x is -2 (negative → left) and y is 5 (positive → up). Left and up land you in which quadrant?

support.prompt: Predict the rectangle area for these settings. Give the answer in square units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: 7 × 6 = 42; perimeter = 26. A (-4, -2), B (3, 4). The displayed distance follows horizontal and vertical streets, not the diagonal.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: A rectangle has opposite corners (−4, −2) and (3, 4). What is its area?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: What is the perimeter of that 7-by-6 rectangle?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The park's marked vertices are 3 units apart and each unit is 100 feet. What is the park's width?
feedback: 3 is the number of UNITS — the scale turns units into feet.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 100.
That adds 3 + 100 instead of multiplying.
hints: What does one unit stand for?
Each unit is 100 feet.

core.prompt: The park's area must be 240,000 sq ft and its width is 300 ft. What is its length?
feedback: 720 comes from 240,000 ÷ 333 or a slip; recompute 240,000 ÷ 300.
That divides by 3 instead of 300 — keep the zeros with the width.
That adds the width to the area — area and length combine by division here.
hints: Area = length × width. Solve for length.
24,000 ÷ 30 is the same division.

core.prompt: The length is 800 feet and each unit represents 100 feet. How many units long is the park on the map?
feedback: That divides by 1,000 instead of 100.
That divides by 10 instead of 100.
That forgets the scale entirely — the map is not drawn in feet.
hints: Feet to units: divide by what one unit stands for.
Move the decimal two places.

core.prompt: The known vertices of the park are at (2, 4) and (5, 4), and the length runs DOWNWARD 8 units. Where are the other two vertices?
core.explanation: 8 units below y = 4 is y = 4 − 8 = −4, keeping each x the same: (2, −4) and (5, −4).
feedback: (2, 12) moves UP 8 units instead of down.
y = −8 would be 12 units below y = 4, not 8.
Those move sideways along x instead of down.
hints: Down means subtract from y.
x-coordinates stay the same.

core.prompt: Sheng plans a zoo visit using a map where exhibits sit at grid points. Explain how identifying WHAT the problem asks (his shortest route? total distance?) changes what you compute.
core.frame: If the question is ___ , I would compute ___ .
core.explanation: If the problem asks total walking distance, I add the distances between the exhibits along his path. If it asks whether one route is shorter than another, I compute both totals and compare. Naming the question first tells me which distances matter.

core.prompt: Point A is at (-5, 3). If you move 8 units to the right, what are the new coordinates?
core.explanation: Moving right means adding to the x-coordinate: -5 + 8 = 3. The y stays the same. New point: (3, 3).
feedback: Not quite. Moving right means adding to the x-coordinate: -5 + 8 = ___.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
hints: Moving right changes ONLY the x-coordinate. The y-coordinate stays at 3.
Add the move to the x-value: take -5 and count up 8. Careful crossing zero — use a number line if it helps.
Start at -5 and count 8 steps right: -4, -3, -2, ... keep going all 8 steps. Then keep the y as 3.

core.prompt: In which quadrant is the point (-3, 5)?
core.explanation: Negative x with positive y places the point in Quadrant II.
feedback: Quadrant I is where x is positive and y is positive. Check the sign of each coordinate in the point and match both.
Quadrant III requires both coordinates to be negative, but 5 is positive.
Quadrant IV needs a positive x-coordinate, and here x is −3.
hints: Check the signs: x = -3 is negative and y = 5 is positive.
Negative x means left of the y-axis; positive y means above the x-axis. Which quadrant is up-and-left?
From the origin move left 3, then up 5. Count quadrants counterclockwise from top-right to name where you land.

core.prompt: What are the coordinates of a point 4 units right and 2 units down from the origin?
core.explanation: Right is +x and down is -y, so the point is (4, -2).
feedback: That is what you get if you changed the sign of both coordinates. Instead: Right is +x and down is -y, so the point is ___.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
The two coordinates are swapped. The first number always describes the horizontal move and the second the vertical move.
hints: Two moves: right 4 (horizontal) and down 2 (vertical). Down means a NEGATIVE y.
Build (x, y): x is the right/left amount with its sign, y is the up/down amount with its sign.
Right 4 gives x = 4 (positive). Now write 'down 2' as a signed y-value and put the two in order.

steps: Problem: Name the quadrant for the point (6, -1).
Student thinking: I'll read the coordinates as (y, x), so I treat this like (-1, 6): the first number -1 is negative (left) and the second number 6 is positive (up).
Student answer: (6, -1) is in Quadrant II.
core.explanation: The order was reversed. In an ordered pair (x, y), x ALWAYS comes first. Here x = 6 (positive → right) and y = -1 (negative → down). Right and down is Quadrant IV, not Quadrant II.
hints: In (6, -1), which number is the x-coordinate — the first or the second?
x = 6 (positive → right) and y = -1 (negative → down). Right and down land you in which quadrant?

core.prompt: Predict the rectangle area for these settings. Give the answer in square units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: 6 × 6 = 36; perimeter = 24. A (-3, -2), B (3, 4). The displayed distance follows horizontal and vertical streets, not the diagonal.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

core.prompt: A rectangle has opposite corners (−4, −2) and (3, 4). What is its area?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: What is the perimeter of that 7-by-6 rectangle?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.

stretch.prompt: Maria is choosing between two store spaces on a grid where each unit is 1 foot and each grid line is 5 feet apart. Space A is a rectangle 25 ft by 40 ft; Space B is 30 ft by 30 ft. Which has more floor area?
choices: Space A — 1,000 sq ft vs 900 sq ft
Space B — 900 sq ft vs 850 sq ft
Space B — because a square always beats a rectangle
stretch.explanation: A: 25 × 40 = 1,000 sq ft. B: 30 × 30 = 900 sq ft. Space A has 100 more square feet.
feedback: B is 900, but A is 1,000 — recompute 25 × 40.
Shape does not decide area; the dimensions do.
hints: Compute each area.

stretch.prompt: A square has vertices (a, b) and (a, b + s) on one side. Which operation gives the side length for ANY values?
choices: Subtract the y-coordinates and take the absolute value
stretch.explanation: Same x means the side is vertical, and |(b + s) − b| = |s| — subtraction with absolute value works for every case.
feedback: Adding coordinates has no geometric meaning here.
A product of coordinates is not a distance.
An average finds a midpoint, not a length.
hints: Which coordinate changes along the side?
Only y changes.
Distance = absolute difference of the changing coordinate.

stretch.prompt: The park design used width from coordinates, then length from the area, then the scale to place the missing vertices. Design your own version: pick an area and a scale, mark two vertices, and show where the other two go.
stretch.frame: My area is ___ and each unit is ___ .
stretch.explanation: My park has area 60,000 sq ft with each unit = 100 ft. I mark vertices at (1, 5) and (3, 5) — 2 units apart, so width 200 ft. Length = 60,000 ÷ 200 = 300 ft = 3 units, so the other vertices go at (1, 2) and (3, 2), 3 units below.

stretch.prompt: A point (a, b) has a < 0 and b < 0. In which quadrant does it lie?
stretch.explanation: Both coordinates negative places the point in Quadrant III.
feedback: Quadrant I is where x is positive and y is positive. Check the sign of each coordinate in the point and match both.
Quadrant II has a negative x but a positive y, and here b is negative too.
Quadrant IV pairs a positive x with a negative y, but a is negative here.
hints: a < 0 means the x is negative; b < 0 means the y is negative — this is a signs question in disguise.
Negative x goes left and negative y goes down. Find the down-and-left region, counting I–IV counterclockwise.
Pick a sample like (-2, -3) and plot it: left 2, down 3. Which region did you land in?

stretch.prompt: Reflecting the point (3, -6) across the x-axis gives which point?
stretch.explanation: Reflecting across the x-axis negates the y-coordinate: (3, -6) → (3, 6).
feedback: That is what you get if you changed the sign of both coordinates — re-read what the question is asking for.
Both coordinates changed sign, which is a reflection across both axes. A reflection across the x-axis leaves the x-coordinate alone.
You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
hints: Reflecting across the x-axis flips a point vertically — up/down changes, left/right doesn't.
The x-coordinate stays the same; the y-coordinate switches sign. Don't swap the order of the two numbers.
Keep the 3. The point sits 6 below the x-axis, so its mirror sits the same 6 units ABOVE. Build that pair.

steps: Student thinking: The x is -3, so I go left 3. The y is -5, so I go up 5.
Student answer: (-3, -5) is in Quadrant II
stretch.explanation: A negative y-coordinate means DOWN, not up. Go left 3 and DOWN 5. The point (-3, -5) is in Quadrant III (both negative), not Quadrant II.
hints: What direction does a NEGATIVE y-coordinate go — up or down?
Both coordinates are negative. In which quadrant are both x and y negative?

stretch.prompt: A point starts in Quadrant I at (4, 6). Describe a move that puts it in Quadrant III. What must happen to both coordinates? Can you give the exact new coordinates after your move?
stretch.frame: To move from Quadrant I to Quadrant III, both coordinates must become ___. Starting at (4, 6), I could move ___ units left and ___ units down to reach (___,___), which is in Quadrant III because ___.
stretch.explanation: Quadrant III is the bottom-left region, so both coordinates have to end up negative. Starting at (4, 6), you need to move more than 4 units left to push x below 0 and more than 6 units down to push y below 0. Moving 6 left and 8 down, for example, lands on (-2, -2), which is Quadrant III because x and y are both negative.
hints: Quadrant III is the bottom-left region — think about what must be true of BOTH signs there.
Plan moves that flip each sign: enough LEFT to push x = 4 below zero, enough DOWN to push y = 6 below zero.
Try moving left MORE than 4 units — say how far x = 4 travels and where it lands. Then plan the down move for y = 6.

stretch.explanation: 5 × 6 = 30; perimeter = 22. A (-2, -2), B (3, 4). The displayed distance follows horizontal and vertical streets, not the diagonal.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.
